Pregnancy Asana Guidance

Gentle movement library

General educational examples only. Ask your obstetric clinician whether prenatal yoga is suitable for you, especially if you have pregnancy complications or activity restrictions. Move gently, breathe normally, and stop if uncomfortable.

🧘 Cat–Cow

Gentle hands-and-knees back mobility.

🌿 Supported Child's Pose

Supported rest, only if belly and breathing remain completely comfortable.

✨ Supported Bound Angle

Seated hip-opening position with cushions; no forced stretch.

Gentle mobility

🧘 Cat–Cow

How to perform

  1. Use a non-slip mat. Come onto hands and knees, hands under shoulders and knees comfortably apart.
  2. Inhale gently, lift your chest slightly and allow a small comfortable arch through your back.
  3. Exhale and gently round your upper back. Let your head follow without forcing your neck.
  4. Move slowly between the two shapes for 4–6 easy cycles while breathing normally.

Modifications

  • Place a folded towel under your knees.
  • Use yoga blocks or fists if your wrists feel uncomfortable.
  • Try the same gentle movement seated, with hands resting on your thighs.

Stop if

You experience pain, dizziness, unusual breathlessness, pelvic pressure, bleeding, fluid leakage, contractions, or any symptom your maternity team has warned you about. Check with your clinician first if you have activity restrictions.

Supported rest

🌿 Supported Child's Pose

How to perform

  1. Kneel on a padded mat with knees comfortably wide, leaving space for your abdomen.
  2. Place a firm bolster or pillows lengthwise in front of you.
  3. Lean your forearms and upper body onto the support only if your belly is completely uncompressed and breathing feels easy.
  4. Stay for 3–5 relaxed breaths, then use your hands to come upright slowly.

Modifications and cautions

  • Raise the support so your chest and abdomen are not pressed down.
  • If kneeling or folding forward feels uncomfortable, skip this pose and rest upright with pillows behind your back.
  • This position may not suit later pregnancy or anyone with reflux, breathlessness, knee pain, pelvic pain, or abdominal pressure. Never force it.

Ask your prenatal clinician if you are unsure whether this position is appropriate.

Seated stretch

✨ Supported Bound Angle

How to perform

  1. Sit on a folded blanket or firm cushion so your hips are slightly higher than your knees.
  2. Bring the soles of your feet together only as close as feels comfortable. Let your knees relax outward naturally.
  3. Place cushions or yoga blocks under your thighs for support. Keep your spine tall and shoulders relaxed.
  4. Rest your hands on your legs or feet. Breathe gently for 5–8 breaths, then use your hands to bring your knees together.

Modifications

  • Move your feet farther away from your body to reduce the stretch.
  • Sit with your back against a wall or on a chair if floor sitting is uncomfortable.
  • Do not press your knees down or bounce them.

Stop if you feel groin, hip, pelvic-girdle, back, or knee pain, numbness, or dizziness. Ask a clinician or prenatal physiotherapist if you have pelvic pain or mobility restrictions.
